chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from Ahmad, from al-Husayn, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Ammar, who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about the woman who was with them on a journey, and she would pray Maghrib as two rak'ahs both going and returning. He said, 'There is no qada (make-up prayer) upon her.'
This is a shadh (anomalous) report, upon which we do not act, because we have clarified that Maghrib is not shortened in it, so whoever shortens it, he must perform i'adah (repetition).

key_terms.الْإِعَادَةُ: Repetition of the prayer within its prescribed time
key_terms.خَبَرٌ شَاذٌّ: An anomalous report where the narrator is reliable but contradicts a more established or numerous report
key_terms.قَضَاءٌ: Make-up prayer performed after the prescribed time has passed
key_terms.يُقَصَّرُ: Shortened (referring to reducing the number of rak'ahs in prayer)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a traveler who shortens the Maghrib prayer during their journey?
ai.summary: In this report from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) rules that a woman praying Maghrib as two rak'ahs during travel is exempt from *qada* (make-up), yet Shaykh al-Tusi classifies this as *shadh* (anomalous) because the prevailing Shia view holds that Maghrib is not shortened but rather repeated (*i'adah*) if prayed as two. This highlights the nuanced distinction between the permissibility of shortening in certain contexts versus the obligatory nature of repeating the full prayer when the standard four-rak'ah structure is altered. The commentary underscores the rigorous methodology of the jurists in reconciling individual reports with established legal principles regarding travel prayers.
